chapter: The Vitaphone film and studio work
title: Sound disc synchronization and how the film compares to The Jazz Singer
summary: Sound and picture were recorded separately and often fell out of sync; the film took three hours and predated The Jazz Singer.

bands.name: Reb Spikes and His Majors and Minors Orchestra

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And I think I read in some of the material that you loaned me...uh, that the sound was recorded on a separate disc and then played with the film in the theater.

Well, sometimes...sometimes they...they would be that far apart, and the music be playing and then no picture [laughs], and then the picture come, and...you know, they were gettin' it together. They were made at the same time but...uh, on different...record player and the picture, and sometimes they got what they call "out-of-sync." If it just that far ahead, you'd be...I'd be up there working my mouth, and the band would off of the picture, so they always...every time they had to get in there and change 'em and get 'em to...uh...synchronize them again, you know what I mean?
Uh huh. And this picture that you made was made in 1927. Is that right?
And "The Jazz Singer" with Al Jolson was made in 1928.
Was "The Jazz Singer", do you know, was it made the same way with the sound on a...on a phonograph disc?
Musta been. Musta been 'cause it was some time before they had 'em all on one, you know.
Uh huh. So how long did it take you to make this film?

Oh, well I 'magine it took us about three hours because, you know, you had to...we tried it out...for sound...and for distance...leveling off...and all like that, you know, so it...we was out there... Now here's something about me that I don't know if you'd want
